# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES physiological logging.** ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al. 1992) logs updates *physiologically*: physical addressing to a page, logical description of the change within the page. Every log record carries a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**; every page carries a **pageLSN** recording the LSN of the last record applied to it. The WAL protocol imposes two invariants: (a) *log-before-data* — a dirty page may not be flushed until all log records up to its pageLSN are durable (enforced via the **flushedLSN**); (b) *force-log-at-commit* — a transaction's commit record must be durable before commit is acknowledged. Per-transaction **prevLSN** chains enable efficient rollback, and **undoNextLSN** pointers in compensation records support partial rollback to savepoints.

**Group commit.** Forcing the log at every commit would bound throughput by fsync latency. Group commit batches the commit records of many concurrent transactions into a single fsync, amortizing the synchronous I/O. InnoDB's redo log and PostgreSQL's `commit_delay`/WAL writer implement variants; modern systems (e.g., Aurora) extend this with asynchronous commit pipelines acknowledging on quorum durability.

**Fuzzy checkpointing.** ARIES-style checkpoints do not quiesce the system. A checkpoint writes the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — each dirty page with its **recLSN** (first LSN that dirtied it) — and the **Active Transaction Table (ATT)**, bounding how far back redo must scan. The checkpoint's location is recorded in a master record so recovery can find it.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes vs. doublewrite buffer.** Because physiological redo requires an internally consistent page image, a partially written ("torn") page is unrecoverable from deltas alone. PostgreSQL writes a **full-page image (FPI)** into WAL on the first modification of each page after a checkpoint; InnoDB instead writes pages first to a sequential **doublewrite buffer**, then to their home locations, so a torn home-page write can be repaired from the doublewrite copy.

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**PostgreSQL append-only tuple versioning.** Each heap tuple carries **xmin** (creating XID) and **xmax** (deleting/updating XID). A snapshot (xmin, xmax, in-progress XID list) plus the CLOG (commit log) determines visibility. Updates create new tuple versions chained by **ctid**; **HOT (Heap-Only Tuple)** updates avoid new index entries when indexed columns are unchanged and the new version fits on the same page. Dead versions are reclaimed by **VACUUM**, which also freezes old XIDs to prevent 32-bit transaction-ID wraparound.

**InnoDB undo-log-based MVCC.** InnoDB updates rows in place and stores before-images in **undo logs** within **rollback segments**. Each record carries **DB_TRX_ID** and **DB_ROLL_PTR**; a reader with a **read view** (snapshot of active transaction IDs) walks the roll-pointer chain backwards, reconstructing the version visible to it. **Purge threads** garbage-collect undo records once no read view can need them — the classic cause of "long-running transaction bloats history length."

**Snapshot Isolation and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain SI (first-committer-wins on write-write conflicts) admits **write skew**: two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint items, producing a non-serializable outcome. **SSI** (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; PostgreSQL ≥9.1) tracks rw-antidependencies with **SIREAD locks** (including predicate/gap coverage) and aborts a transaction when it becomes the **pivot** of two consecutive rw-antidependency edges ("dangerous structure"), which is a necessary condition for an SI anomaly.

**Timestamp-ordered in-memory MVCC (Hekaton).** Microsoft Hekaton stamps versions with begin/end timestamps, uses optimistic validation (read-set revalidation at commit), lock-free Bw-tree/hash indexes, and cooperative garbage collection — no latches, no in-place updates.

## 3. Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees

**Memtable + SSTable architecture.** Writes go to a WAL plus an in-memory **memtable** (typically a skiplist). When full, it is frozen as an immutable memtable and flushed as a sorted, immutable **SSTable** with a sparse index and **fence pointers** (block-level min/max keys) enabling binary search to a single block. Reads merge memtable and SSTables, newest first; deletes are logical **tombstones** that must survive compaction until they reach the bottom level (Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` guards against tombstone loss resurrecting data).

**Leveled vs. size-tiered compaction.** **Leveled compaction (LCS, RocksDB default)** maintains levels L1…Ln of exponentially increasing size with non-overlapping SSTables per level; compaction merges one SSTable into the overlapping range of the next level. This minimizes space amplification (~1.1×) and read amplification but incurs high write amplification (~10× per level). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS, Cassandra default)** merges SSTables of similar size into bigger ones: low write amplification, but high space amplification (up to 2×+ transient) and more tables per read. **Time-windowed compaction (TWCS)** buckets SSTables by time window for TTL'd time-series data so whole SSTables expire atomically.

**Bloom filters and amplification tradeoffs.** Per-SSTable **Bloom filters** (~10 bits/key → ~1% false positives) let point lookups skip tables without I/O; **Monkey** (Dayan et al.) shows optimal bits-per-key should vary by level. The **RUM conjecture** formalizes the three-way tradeoff: no structure simultaneously minimizes Read, Update (write), and Memory/space amplification — LSMs trade read amplification for write throughput, the inverse of B+trees.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Splits, merges, and rebalancing.** Insertion into a full leaf splits it, promoting a separator key to the parent; splits propagate upward and may grow the tree at the root (the only way height increases). Deletion below the minimum fill factor triggers **borrowing (redistribution)** from a sibling or a **merge (coalescing)** with separator demotion. Many production engines (e.g., InnoDB) defer merges lazily, tolerating under-full pages to avoid split/merge thrashing.

**Latch coupling (crabbing) and Lehman–Yao B-link trees.** Concurrent traversal uses **latch coupling**: hold the parent latch until the child latch is acquired, releasing early if the child is "safe" (won't split/merge). The **B-link tree** (Lehman & Yao 1981) adds a **high key** and a **right-sibling pointer** to every node: a split first creates the right sibling, so a concurrent reader finding a key greater than the high key simply chases the sibling link — permitting lock-free right traversal and at most one latch held during descent. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao variant.

**Fill-factor heuristics and key compression.** A naïve 50/50 split halves utilization under monotonically increasing keys (sequential inserts), so engines special-case rightmost-leaf splits: InnoDB splits ~90/10 at the insertion point for sequential patterns; PostgreSQL applies a rightmost-leaf fillfactor. **Suffix truncation** stores only the shortest separator distinguishing left from right in internal nodes; **prefix compression** elides shared leading bytes within a page — both raise fanout and reduce height. (Latch-free alternative: the **Bw-tree** uses delta records and a mapping table with CAS installs instead of in-place updates.)

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**Basic protocol with forced logging.** The coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant acquires all needed locks, **force-writes a prepare record**, and votes YES (entering the *in-doubt* state) or NO. On unanimous YES the coordinator force-writes a **commit record** (the commit point), then sends COMMIT; participants write commit records and ACK. 2PC's defining weakness is **blocking**: if the coordinator fails after participants prepare, they must hold locks until it recovers — safety is preserved, liveness is not.

**Presumed abort / presumed commit.** **Presumed abort** (the R* optimization, industry standard, e.g., XA): the coordinator writes no abort record and participants need not ACK aborts; on inquiry about an unknown transaction, the answer is "abort." Read-only participants vote READ-ONLY and skip phase two entirely. **Presumed commit** inverts the default to save messages on the (common) commit path but requires the coordinator to force-log the participant list *before* prepare.

**Three-phase commit (3PC).** Skeen's 3PC inserts a **pre-commit** phase so no participant commits until all are known to be prepared, making the protocol non-blocking under a synchronous, crash-stop (no partition) model. Under network partitions 3PC can violate safety, which is why it is rarely deployed.

**Paxos Commit / consensus-replicated coordination.** Gray & Lamport's **Paxos Commit** replicates each participant's vote via a Paxos instance, removing the coordinator as a single point of failure. **Google Spanner** embodies the practical pattern: 2PC runs *across* Paxos groups, with the coordinator's state itself replicated by Paxos, so coordinator failover eliminates the blocking window; commit timestamps come from TrueTime.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport clocks.** A scalar counter per process: increment on local events; on receive, set `C := max(C_local, C_msg) + 1`. Guarantees `a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b)` (consistency with happened-before), but not the converse — concurrent events are not detectable. Lamport timestamps + process-ID tiebreak yield a total order, the basis of distributed mutual exclusion and timestamp-ordering concurrency control.

**Vector clocks and version vectors.** A vector `V[1..n]`, one slot per process: `V_a < V_b ⇔ a → b`, and incomparable vectors identify **concurrent** events exactly. **Version vectors** apply this per data item to detect conflicting replica siblings (Dynamo/early Riak); **dotted version vectors** fix sibling explosion under server-side ID assignment by attaching a precise "dot" (event identifier) per write. Cost: O(n) metadata, pruning difficulties with churning membership.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni et al. 2014) combines physical time with a logical component: timestamps stay within a bounded offset of physical NTP time while preserving the happened-before property of Lamport clocks, and fit in 64 bits. **CockroachDB** uses HLC for MVCC timestamps and causality propagation across sessions; the contrast is **Spanner's TrueTime**, which uses GPS/atomic-clock-bounded uncertainty intervals and **commit wait** to achieve external consistency via real hardware rather than logical causality tracking.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Majority read/write quorums (R + W > N).** With N replicas, requiring W write acks and R read acks such that `R + W > N` guarantees read/write quorum intersection, so every read sees at least one latest-write replica (per-key version numbers resolve which). `W + W > N` prevents conflicting concurrent writes. Note this gives *regular register*-style guarantees, not linearizability, without read-repair or consensus on top.

**Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff (Dynamo).** When home replicas are unreachable, Dynamo-style systems (Cassandra, Riak) write to the next healthy nodes on the ring with a **hint**; the stand-in later hands the data off to the home node. This maximizes write availability but breaks strict quorum intersection — a sloppy-quorum read may miss a sloppy-quorum write — so it trades consistency for availability. Complemented by **read repair** and **anti-entropy via Merkle trees**.

**Consensus majority quorums and Flexible Paxos.** Raft and (Multi-)Paxos use majority quorums for both leader election and log replication; any two majorities intersect, so a new leader is guaranteed to see every committed entry (Raft additionally restricts votes to candidates with up-to-date logs). **Flexible Paxos** (Howard et al. 2016) relaxes this: only election quorums (Q1) and replication quorums (Q2) need intersect, enabling e.g. small fast-path replication quorums with large election quorums. **Witness replicas** (log-only, data-less voters; used in Spanner and CockroachDB) cheapen quorum membership for tie-breaking across regions.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** (1) **Analysis**: scan forward from the last checkpoint, reconstructing the DPT and ATT, determining losers (uncommitted at crash). (2) **Redo — "repeat history"**: from the minimum recLSN, re-apply *all* updates (including those of losers) where `pageLSN < record LSN`, restoring the exact pre-crash state — the key insight enabling fine-grained physiological logging. (3) **Undo**: roll back losers by following prevLSN chains, writing a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)** for each undone action; CLRs are redo-only and carry **undoNextLSN**, making recovery idempotent and bounded even across repeated crashes during recovery.

**Shadow paging.** The System R alternative: updates go to shadow copies of pages; commit atomically swaps the root/page-table pointer, so recovery is trivial (discard shadows). Costs — destroyed clustering, page-granularity copy-on-write, hard concurrency at a single root — made WAL dominant, though CoW B-trees in LMDB and ZFS/Btrfs are its modern descendants (LMDB needs no WAL at all).

**LSM recovery: WAL replay + MANIFEST.** RocksDB-style engines recover by (a) replaying the WAL to rebuild memtables lost at crash (sync policy determines the durability window), and (b) reading the **MANIFEST**, a log of **VersionEdits** recording every SSTable add/delete per level, to reconstruct the exact LSM shape; orphaned SSTables from half-finished compactions are simply garbage-collected since SSTables are immutable. Immutability converts most crash states into "ignore the incomplete file."

**Checkpoint-coupled bounds.** In all three designs, checkpointing (fuzzy DPT/ATT snapshots in ARIES, memtable flush + WAL truncation in LSMs, root-pointer commit in shadow/CoW systems) bounds recovery time — the universal engineering lever is trading steady-state write overhead for recovery-scan length.

---

**Synthesis.** The unifying themes: (i) *durability is a logging discipline* — WAL ordering invariants (ARIES) or structural immutability (LSM, shadow paging) make redo/undo well-defined; (ii) *isolation is a versioning discipline* — MVCC variants differ chiefly in where old versions live (heap, undo log, delta chains) and how they're reclaimed; (iii) *distribution is an intersection discipline* — 2PC, quorums, and consensus all derive safety from forced durable state plus overlapping participant sets, with logical/hybrid clocks supplying the ordering that physical clocks cannot guarantee.

Answer: The complete technical brief above covers all eight areas with ≥3 named mechanisms each — WAL (ARIES physiological logging/LSNs, group commit, fuzzy checkpoints, full-page writes vs. doublewrite buffer); MVCC (PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+HOT+VACUUM, InnoDB undo-log read views, SSI with SIREAD locks, Hekaton); LSM trees (memtable/SSTable+fence pointers, leveled vs. size-tiered vs. time-windowed compaction, Bloom filters/RUM tradeoffs, tombstones); B+tree maintenance (split/merge/redistribution, latch crabbing and Lehman–Yao B-link trees, suffix truncation and sequential-insert split heuristics); 2PC (forced prepare/commit logging, presumed abort/commit, 3PC, Paxos Commit/Spanner); logical clocks (Lamport, vector/dotted version vectors, HLC vs. TrueTime); quorums (R+W>N majority quorums, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, Raft/Flexible-Paxos quorums and witnesses); and crash recovery (ARIES analysis/redo/undo with CLRs, shadow paging, RocksDB WAL+MANIFEST replay).

response.content:
# Write-Ahead Logging and Crash Recovery: Technical Findings

---

## Part 1: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

### 1.1 The WAL Protocol (Core Invariants)

The write-ahead logging protocol consists of two rules that together guarantee the **durability (D)** and **atomicity (A)** properties of ACID under a no-force/steal buffer management policy:

1. **Log-before-data (the WAL rule proper):** Before a dirty page may be flushed from the buffer pool to the stable database, all log records describing updates to that page — up to and including the page's `pageLSN` — must first be forced to stable storage. Formally: `flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN` is required before the page write is permitted. This enables **UNDO** of uncommitted changes that reached disk (necessary because of the **steal** policy, which allows eviction of dirty pages from uncommitted transactions).

2. **Force-log-at-commit (commit rule):** A transaction is not considered committed until its commit log record (and all preceding log records of that transaction) are durably flushed to the log. This enables **REDO** of committed changes that never reached the data files (necessary because of the **no-force** policy, which does not require flushing dirty pages at commit).

The **steal/no-force** combination is the standard high-performance policy; WAL is precisely the mechanism that makes it safe. The alternative quadrants (no-steal/force) avoid undo/redo respectively but perform poorly.

### 1.2 ARIES Physiological Logging, LSNs, and pageLSN

**ARIES** (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al., IBM, 1992) uses **physiological logging**: log records are *physical to a page, logical within a page*. A record identifies the page ID and describes the operation (e.g., "insert tuple with these bytes into slot array of page P"), rather than a pure physical byte-diff of the whole page (too large) or a pure logical operation like "insert into table T" (not idempotent, hard to redo when physical layout changed). Physiological logging makes redo **page-oriented and idempotent-via-LSN-check**, while undo can be logical (important when the tuple has moved pages).

Key data structures:

- **LSN (Log Sequence Number):** a monotonically increasing identifier of a log record, typically the record's byte offset in the log, giving a total order on log records.
- **pageLSN:** stored in each page header; the LSN of the most recent log record that modified that page. During redo, the rule is: apply the logged update **iff `pageLSN < LSN` of the record** — this makes redo idempotent even across repeated crashes during recovery.
- **prevLSN:** each log record points to the previous log record of the same transaction, forming a per-transaction backward chain used for undo.
- **flushedLSN:** in-memory marker of the last log record durably on disk; enforces the WAL rule.
- **recLSN (recovery LSN):** per dirty page, the LSN of the first record that dirtied it since it was last flushed — recorded in the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** and used to compute the redo start point.
- **Transaction Table (TT / ATT):** tracks active transactions, their state, and `lastLSN`.

Log record types: UPDATE, COMMIT, ABORT, END, **CLR** (compensation log record — see recovery), and checkpoint records (BEGIN_CHECKPOINT / END_CHECKPOINT).

### 1.3 Group Commit

Force-log-at-commit implies one log `fsync` per commit, which would bottleneck throughput on device sync latency. **Group commit** amortizes this: the log manager batches commit records from multiple concurrently committing transactions and flushes them with a **single fsync**, then releases all waiters whose commit LSN ≤ flushedLSN. Implementations:

- **PostgreSQL:** `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings` plus an inherent batching effect — backends waiting on the WAL flush lock piggyback on the leader's flush (leader-based group commit on `WALWriteLock`).
- **MySQL/InnoDB binary-log group commit (BLGC):** a staged leader–follower pipeline (flush stage → sync stage → commit stage) that also preserves binlog/InnoDB commit ordering for replication consistency.
- A related relaxation is **asynchronous commit** (PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit = off`, InnoDB `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 0/2`), which trades a bounded window of durability loss for latency — distinct from group commit, which preserves full durability.

### 1.4 Checkpointing — Fuzzy Checkpoints

Checkpoints bound recovery time by limiting how far back log analysis/redo must scan.

- **Sharp (consistent) checkpoint:** quiesce updates and flush all dirty pages — simple but stalls the system; impractical for large buffer pools.
- **Fuzzy checkpoint (ARIES):** no quiescing. Write a BEGIN_CHECKPOINT record; then write an END_CHECKPOINT record containing a **snapshot of the Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table**. Dirty pages are *not* flushed synchronously; they are written back lazily by background writers. The LSN of the BEGIN_CHECKPOINT (the **master record**, stored at a known location) anchors recovery. The redo start point is then `min(recLSN)` over the checkpointed DPT — which may be *earlier* than the checkpoint LSN itself. Because the system keeps running, the checkpoint reflects a "fuzzy" in-flight state; correctness is restored by the analysis pass.
- **PostgreSQL** checkpoints are conceptually different (it flushes all dirty buffers, spread over time — "spread checkpoints" governed by `checkpoint_completion_target`), after which WAL before the redo pointer can be recycled. **InnoDB** uses fuzzy checkpointing with a `checkpoint_lsn` advanced as the flush list (ordered by oldest modification LSN) is drained.

### 1.5 Torn-Page Protection: PostgreSQL Full-Page Writes vs. InnoDB Doublewrite Buffer

A **torn page** (partial write) occurs when a database page (8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB) is larger than the storage device's atomic write unit (traditionally a 512 B or 4 KB sector), and a crash mid-write leaves a page that is part-old, part-new. Physiological redo cannot repair such a page, because redo assumes the page is internally consistent at *some* pageLSN. Two standard countermeasures:

- **PostgreSQL full-page writes (FPW):** with `full_page_writes = on`, the **first modification of each page after a checkpoint** logs the *entire page image* into WAL (a full-page image, FPI) instead of just the delta. During recovery, a torn page is simply overwritten wholesale by the FPI, and subsequent deltas apply on top. Cost: WAL volume spikes right after each checkpoint (motivating longer checkpoint intervals and `wal_compression`). Protection lives *in the log stream*.
- **InnoDB doublewrite buffer:** before writing dirty pages to their final locations in the tablespace, InnoDB first writes them **sequentially to a dedicated doublewrite area** (separate `.dblwr` files since MySQL 8.0.20; previously in the system tablespace), fsyncs, then writes to the final in-place locations. On recovery, any page whose checksum is invalid (torn) is restored from its intact copy in the doublewrite buffer, after which normal redo proceeds. Cost: ~2× page write I/O volume (though sequential batch writes keep the overhead modest, typically <10%). Protection lives *in the data path*, keeping the redo log compact (InnoDB logs only deltas).

Both can be disabled safely only on storage guaranteeing atomic writes at page granularity (e.g., ZFS with matching recordsize, or devices/filesystems supporting atomic 16 KB writes, as exploited by `innodb_doublewrite = OFF` on capable hardware).

---

## Part 2: Crash Recovery

### 2.1 ARIES Three-Phase Recovery

On restart after a crash, ARIES locates the most recent checkpoint via the master record and runs three sequential passes:

**Phase 1 — Analysis.** Scan forward from the BEGIN_CHECKPOINT record to the end of the log. Reconstruct:
- the **Transaction Table**: transactions with no END record are **losers** (to be undone); those with COMMIT but no END are winners needing only an END record;
- the **Dirty Page Table**: pages possibly dirty at crash time, each with its recLSN.
Output: the set of loser transactions and `redoLSN = min(recLSN over DPT)` — the redo scan start point.

**Phase 2 — Redo ("repeating history").** Scan forward from `redoLSN`, and **reapply every logged update — including updates of loser transactions and even CLRs** — subject to the conditions: the page is in the DPT, `recLSN ≤ LSN`, and after fetching the page, `pageLSN < LSN`. This is ARIES's signature principle, **repeating history before undo**: the database is restored to its *exact* state at the instant of the crash, including uncommitted changes. This is what makes ARIES work with fine-grained (record-level) locking and physiological logging, because undo then operates on exactly the state the original transactions saw. Redo is idempotent via the pageLSN comparison.

**Phase 3 — Undo.** Roll back all loser transactions by scanning **backward** through the log, processing the record with the maximal LSN among all losers' `lastLSN` chains (following prevLSN pointers), until every loser's chain is exhausted; then write an END record per loser. Undo of an update may be **logical** (e.g., delete the key that was inserted), tolerating the tuple having moved pages since.

**CLRs (Compensation Log Records).** Every undo action is itself logged as a CLR. A CLR:
- is **redo-only** — it is never undone (preventing unbounded log growth if crashes recur during recovery);
- carries an **undoNextLSN** pointer: the prevLSN of the record just compensated, i.e., the next record to undo. If the system crashes during undo and recovers again, undo resumes at undoNextLSN, skipping already-compensated records. This guarantees **bounded, non-repeating rollback work** across arbitrarily many crashes during recovery, and allows normal transaction rollback (ABORT) to use the identical mechanism.

Additional ARIES features worth naming: support for **partial rollback via savepoints**, **nested top actions** (e.g., B-tree page splits that must survive even if the enclosing transaction aborts — implemented with a dummy CLR bridging over the action), and fuzzy checkpointing during the undo pass itself.

### 2.2 Shadow Paging (Alternative to WAL)

**Shadow paging** (classically System R's shadow mechanism; Lorie 1977) achieves atomicity without a redo/undo log for data:

- The database is accessed through a **page table / page map**. Updates are **copy-on-write**: a modified page is written to a fresh disk location (the *current* version), while the *shadow* copy of the page table continues to reference the old pages.
- **Commit** = atomically installing the new page table as the root (a single atomic pointer/root-block swap). **Abort/crash recovery** = simply discarding current pages and reverting to the shadow page table — recovery is near-instantaneous with no redo or undo passes.

Drawbacks that led the industry to ARIES-style WAL instead: commit requires flushing data pages (effectively a **force** policy); copy-on-write destroys **physical clustering/locality** and fragments the file; garbage collection of superseded pages is required; the page-table root becomes a commit bottleneck; and page-level granularity complicates concurrent fine-grained transactions. Modern descendants: **LMDB** (copy-on-write B+-tree with two root metapages, no WAL), **SQLite in rollback-journal mode** is a related before-image scheme (though SQLite's WAL mode is, as named, write-ahead logging), and CoW filesystems (ZFS, Btrfs) apply the same principle at the FS layer.

### 2.3 LSM-Tree / RocksDB Recovery: WAL Replay + MANIFEST

LSM-tree engines (RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra's commitlog, and by extension MyRocks) use WAL differently from in-place-update engines, and their recovery has **two cooperating mechanisms**:

**(a) WAL replay for the MemTable.** Every write (Put/Delete/Merge, batched atomically as a `WriteBatch` tagged with a **sequence number** — the LSM analogue of an LSN) is appended to the WAL *before* insertion into the in-memory **MemTable**. Because all persistent SST files are **immutable** and written only via whole-file flush/compaction (never updated in place), the WAL's sole recovery job is to **reconstruct the contents of MemTables lost at crash**. On recovery, RocksDB replays live WAL segments in order, rebuilding MemTables; a WAL segment becomes obsolete only once the MemTables it covers are flushed to SSTs **and** that flush is durably recorded. WAL records are framed with per-block **CRC32C checksums**; a corrupt/torn tail is handled per `wal_recovery_mode` (e.g., `kPointInTimeRecovery`, the default: replay up to the first corruption, truncating the suffix — note there is **no torn-page problem for SSTs**, since append-only immutable files make partial writes detectable and discardable). Durability per write is governed by `WriteOptions.sync` (fsync per batch vs. periodic `wal_bytes_per_sync`).

**(b) MANIFEST recovery for the LSM version state.** The set of live SST files, their key ranges, levels, and the current log number/sequence number constitute a **Version**. Changes to this state (flush adds an SST; compaction adds and deletes SSTs) are recorded as **VersionEdit** records appended to the **MANIFEST** — itself a write-ahead log *of metadata*. A **CURRENT** file atomically names the active MANIFEST. Recovery sequence:
1. Read CURRENT → open MANIFEST → replay VersionEdits to reconstruct the latest Version (the LSM shape) and the last sequence number and minimum live WAL number.
2. Replay the live WALs (step a) from that point to rebuild MemTables.
3. Optionally flush recovered MemTables; obsolete files not referenced by the recovered Version are garbage-collected.

This is effectively a **two-level logging architecture**: data WAL for unflushed user writes, MANIFEST log for file-set metadata — with atomicity of metadata transitions provided by the CURRENT pointer swap (a shadow-paging-like atomic root install, interestingly). Crucially, LSM recovery needs **no undo phase at all**: uncommitted data never reaches SSTs in a way that requires compensation; atomicity is at WriteBatch granularity, and anything after the last valid WAL record is simply absent.

### 2.4 Comparative Summary of the Three Recovery Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Redo needed | Undo needed | Commit cost | Recovery cost | Buffer policy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ARIES (WAL, physiological)** | Yes (repeat history from min recLSN) | Yes (losers, via CLRs) | Log force only (group commit) | Proportional to log since checkpoint (3 passes) | Steal / no-force |
| **Shadow paging** | No | No (discard current pages) | Force data pages + atomic root swap | Near-zero | No-steal / force (effectively) |
| **LSM WAL + MANIFEST (RocksDB)** | Yes (rebuild MemTables + replay VersionEdits) | No | Log append (+optional fsync) | Proportional to unflushed WAL + MANIFEST size | Append-only, immutable files (no in-place steal problem) |

**Named mechanisms delivered — WAL side:** ARIES physiological logging with LSN/pageLSN, the WAL protocol (log-before-data + force-log-at-commit), group commit, fuzzy checkpointing, PostgreSQL full-page writes, InnoDB doublewrite buffer. **Recovery side:** ARIES three-phase recovery (analysis/redo/undo) with repeating history and CLRs, shadow paging, RocksDB WAL replay with MANIFEST/VersionEdit/CURRENT recovery.

# Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) and Logical Clocks

---

## Part 1: MVCC

MVCC is a concurrency-control technique in which writers create new versions of data items rather than overwriting in place, and readers are served a consistent *snapshot* of the database without blocking (or being blocked by) writers. The core invariants: readers never block writers, writers never block readers; write-write conflicts still require coordination (locks, first-committer-wins, or timestamp validation). The costs are version-chain traversal, visibility checks, and garbage collection of dead versions.

### 1.1 PostgreSQL: In-place tuple versioning (xmin/xmax, snapshots, HOT, VACUUM)

**Storage model.** PostgreSQL stores *all* tuple versions in the main heap (an "old-to-new in-heap" design — no separate undo segment). Each heap tuple header carries system columns:

- **`xmin`**: the transaction ID (XID, a 32-bit counter) of the inserting transaction.
- **`xmax`**: the XID of the deleting/updating transaction (0 if the tuple is live). An `UPDATE` is physically a `DELETE` + `INSERT`: the old tuple gets `xmax` set, and a new tuple is written with a fresh `xmin`.
- **`ctid`**: the tuple's physical address (block, offset). In an updated tuple, `ctid` points to the successor version, forming a forward-linked **version chain**.
- **`cmin`/`cmax`**: command IDs for intra-transaction visibility (so a statement doesn't see its own in-progress changes incorrectly — relevant to the Halloween problem).
- **Hint bits** (`HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, `HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED`, etc.) cache commit/abort status to avoid repeated lookups in the **commit log (`pg_xact`/clog)**, which records two bits of status per XID.

**Snapshots and visibility.** At the start of each statement (READ COMMITTED) or at the first statement of the transaction (REPEATABLE READ / SERIALIZABLE), the backend takes a **snapshot** consisting of:
- `xmin` (snapshot): the oldest XID still running — anything older is definitively committed or aborted.
- `xmax` (snapshot): the next XID to be assigned — anything ≥ this is invisible (in the future).
- `xip[]`: the list of in-progress XIDs at snapshot time.

A tuple is visible iff its inserting `xmin` is committed and *not* in-progress per the snapshot, and its `xmax` is either null, aborted, or belongs to a transaction invisible to the snapshot. This is the classic *snapshot isolation* visibility test.

**HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates.** Normally, every new tuple version requires inserting a new index entry in *every* index on the table (PostgreSQL indexes point to physical heap TIDs, and indexes are not versioned). A **HOT update** avoids this when (a) no indexed column changed, and (b) the new version fits on the same heap page. The new version is reached by following the `ctid` chain from the old line pointer; the index entry continues to point at the chain root (via *line-pointer redirection*). HOT also enables cheap intra-page pruning: dead chain members can be reclaimed by any backend during page access, without a full VACUUM.

**VACUUM and wraparound.** Dead tuples (invisible to all current and future snapshots, i.e., with `xmax` older than the global `xmin` horizon / `oldest removable XID`) must be garbage-collected:
- **(Auto)VACUUM** removes dead tuples, reclaims line pointers, updates the **free space map** and **visibility map** (the latter enables index-only scans and lets vacuum skip all-visible pages).
- **Freezing**: because XIDs are 32-bit and compared with modular (circular) arithmetic, old tuples must be *frozen* (marked `FrozenTransactionId` / `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`) before the XID counter wraps; failure leads to **transaction-ID wraparound**, which PostgreSQL prevents with aggressive anti-wraparound autovacuum and, ultimately, by refusing new XIDs.
- **Long-running transactions / stale replication slots** hold back the xmin horizon, causing **bloat** (dead versions that cannot be reclaimed).

**Write-write conflicts.** Under REPEATABLE READ (SI), an update to a row already updated by a concurrent committed transaction fails with a serialization error — **first-updater-wins** semantics (the second updater blocks on the row lock, then aborts if the first commits).

### 1.2 InnoDB (MySQL): Undo-log-based MVCC with read views and rollback segments

InnoDB takes the opposite physical approach: **new-to-old, out-of-place**. The clustered index (the table itself, organized by primary key) always holds the *newest* version in place; prior versions are reconstructed from **undo logs**.

**Record format.** Each clustered-index record carries hidden columns:
- **`DB_TRX_ID`** (6 bytes): ID of the last transaction that inserted or modified the record.
- **`DB_ROLL_PTR`** (7 bytes): a **roll pointer** into the undo log record that can reconstruct the previous version. Chained roll pointers form the version chain, walked backward in time.
- **`DB_ROW_ID`**: synthetic row ID if no PK is defined.

**Undo logs and rollback segments.** Undo records live in **rollback segments** within the undo tablespaces, split into **insert undo** (purgeable immediately at commit — an aborted insert just disappears) and **update undo** (needed for consistent reads, purgeable only when no read view can require them). A background **purge** thread (InnoDB's analogue of VACUUM) removes undo records and physically deletes **delete-marked** records once they fall below the oldest active read view. Long-running transactions cause **history list length** growth — the undo-log analogue of PostgreSQL bloat.

**Read views.** A **read view** is InnoDB's snapshot structure: it records the set of active transaction IDs (`m_ids`), the low-water mark (`up_limit_id`, below which everything is committed), and the high-water mark (`low_limit_id`). Visibility: a record version with `DB_TRX_ID` < up_limit_id is visible; ≥ low_limit_id or in `m_ids` is invisible, so the reader follows `DB_ROLL_PTR` into undo to rebuild an older version.
- **REPEATABLE READ** (InnoDB default): one read view for the whole transaction (plus **next-key locks** — record lock + gap lock — for *locking reads* to prevent phantoms; note this hybrid means plain SELECTs use MVCC snapshots while `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` uses current-read locking, which can produce non-obvious anomalies).
- **READ COMMITTED**: a fresh read view per statement; gap locking is mostly disabled.

Secondary index records don't carry `DB_TRX_ID` per record (only a per-page `PAGE_MAX_TRX_ID`); covered queries may need a clustered-index lookup to check visibility.

### 1.3 Snapshot Isolation anomalies and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

**Snapshot isolation (SI)** gives each transaction a static snapshot plus first-committer-wins (or first-updater-wins) on write-write conflicts. SI forbids dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, lost updates, and (read-only) phantoms — but it is **not serializable**.

**Write skew.** The canonical SI anomaly: two transactions read overlapping data, make disjoint writes based on what they read, and both commit (no write-write conflict), yet the result matches no serial order. Example: constraint "at least one doctor on call." T1 reads both doctors on call, takes Alice off; T2 concurrently reads the same snapshot, takes Bob off. Both commit → zero on call. Related: **read-only transaction anomaly** (Fekete et al.), where even a read-only transaction can observe a state inconsistent with any serial order.

**Theory.** Adya-style serialization graphs: SI anomalies always involve a **dangerous structure** — two consecutive **rw-antidependency** edges ("rw-conflicts": T1 reads something T2 concurrently writes) between concurrent transactions, with the pivot transaction in the middle (Fekete et al., 2005).

**SSI** (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; shipped in PostgreSQL 9.1 as `SERIALIZABLE`) runs SI and additionally detects dangerous structures at runtime:
- Readers take **SIREAD locks** — *non-blocking* predicate/range markers (on tuples, pages, or relations, with lock-escalation to bound memory) recording what was read. They persist past commit until concurrent transactions finish.
- The engine tracks incoming/outgoing rw-antidependencies per transaction. When a transaction accumulates both an **in**-conflict and an **out**-conflict (a pivot in T1 →rw T2 →rw T3), one participant is aborted with a **serialization failure** (clients must retry). This is conservative — false positives abort some actually-serializable executions — but sound.
- Optimization: `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` waits for a **safe snapshot** so a read-only transaction can never be aborted or cause aborts.

### 1.4 Hekaton and timestamp-ordered MVCC

**Hekaton** (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP; Diaconu et al., SIGMOD 2013) is a fully in-memory, lock-free, latch-free MVCC engine:

- **Version layout.** Each version carries a **Begin** and **End timestamp** defining its validity interval `[Begin, End)`. A version is visible to a transaction with read timestamp RT iff `Begin ≤ RT < End`. Versions are immutable once created; updates append a new version and set the old version's End field (initially to the updater's transaction ID as a placeholder, atomically via CAS — the End field doubles as a write lock).
- **Timestamps.** A transaction gets a read/begin timestamp at start and a monotonically increasing **commit timestamp** at the end from a global counter (atomic fetch-and-increment). On commit, the transaction's ID placeholders in Begin/End fields are replaced by its commit timestamp (post-processing).
- **Optimistic multiversion scheme.** For SERIALIZABLE, transactions perform **validation** at commit: re-check read-set visibility (reads still return the same versions at the commit timestamp) and repeat scans to detect phantoms — i.e., validating that the transaction could have run entirely at its commit timestamp. SI needs no read validation. **Commit dependencies** allow speculative reads of uncommitted-but-validating versions, with cascaded abort if the dependency fails.
- **Indexes** are lock-free (Bw-tree and lock-free hash tables); garbage collection is cooperative and parallel, reclaiming versions whose End timestamp precedes the oldest active transaction.

**Timestamp-ordered MVCC generally (MVTO).** In classic **multiversion timestamp ordering**, each transaction gets a start timestamp TS(T); reads return the version with the largest write-timestamp ≤ TS(T) and update the version's read-timestamp; a write is rejected (abort) if a younger transaction already read the version it would supersede. Modern descendants include MVTO/MVOCC hybrids studied in Wu et al.'s "An Empirical Evaluation of In-Memory MVCC" (VLDB 2017), and systems like **HyPer** (MVOCC with precision locking) and **MemSQL/SingleStore**. CockroachDB and Spanner also layer MVCC over timestamp ordering, with timestamps supplied by HLC/TrueTime (below) — connecting the two halves of this report.

**Design-axis summary.** Version storage: append-to-heap (PostgreSQL) vs. delta/undo (InnoDB) vs. in-memory append-only (Hekaton). Version ordering: oldest-to-newest vs. newest-to-oldest chains. Concurrency protocol: MV2PL, MVTO, MVOCC, SI+SSI. Garbage collection: VACUUM, purge threads, cooperative epoch-based GC.

---

## Part 2: Logical Clocks

Logical clocks assign timestamps to events in a distributed system so that causal (happens-before) relationships can be inferred without synchronized physical clocks.

### 2.1 Lamport clocks (scalar logical clocks)

Lamport (1978) defined the **happens-before** relation **→**: the smallest strict partial order such that (a) if a and b are events in the same process and a precedes b, then a → b; (b) if a is a message send and b its receive, a → b; (c) transitivity. Events not ordered by → are **concurrent** (a ∥ b).

**Algorithm.** Each process keeps a counter C:
1. Before each local event: `C := C + 1`.
2. On send: piggyback C on the message.
3. On receive with timestamp T: `C := max(C, T) + 1`.

**Property.** **Clock condition**: a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b). This is only an implication — the converse fails: C(a) < C(b) does *not* imply a → b. Lamport clocks therefore *cannot detect concurrency*; two concurrent events may have any ordering of timestamps. Ties are broken by process ID to get a **total order** consistent with causality — the basis of Lamport's mutual-exclusion algorithm and of totally-ordered multicast / state-machine replication.

### 2.2 Vector clocks, version vectors, and dotted version vectors

**Vector clocks** (Fidge 1988, Mattern 1989) strengthen Lamport clocks to *characterize* causality. Each of N processes keeps a vector V[1..N]:
1. Local event at process i: `V[i] += 1`.
2. Send: attach V.
3. Receive V′ at i: `V[j] := max(V[j], V′[j]) ∀j`, then `V[i] += 1`.

Ordering: V(a) < V(b) iff V(a)[k] ≤ V(b)[k] for all k and strict somewhere. **Key theorem**: a → b ⟺ V(a) < V(b), and a ∥ b ⟺ V(a) and V(b) are incomparable. Vector clocks thus *detect* concurrency exactly. Cost: O(N) space per timestamp; Charron-Bost (1991) proved Θ(N) entries are necessary to capture causality in general — the fundamental scalability limit. Uses: causal broadcast/causal consistency (e.g., COPS), distributed debugging, consistent global snapshots.

**Version vectors** (Parker et al. 1983, for detecting mutual inconsistency in replicated files) are the data-replication specialization: one entry per *replica*, incremented per *update* (not per event), used to compare *object versions* — dominance means one version supersedes another; incomparability means a **conflict** requiring reconciliation (siblings). Amazon **Dynamo** used version vectors per key, returning sibling versions to clients for semantic merge. A known hazard with *client-id-based* vectors is unbounded growth; with *server-id-based* vectors, the hazard is **false concurrency / sibling explosion and lost-update risk** when multiple clients write through the same replica.

**Dotted version vectors (DVV)** (Preguiça, Baquero et al., 2010/2012; adopted by Riak) fix the server-side-vector problem. A DVV is a version vector plus a **dot** — a single discrete event identifier `(replica, counter)` naming the exact write event that created this version, separate from the contiguous causal history in the vector. This lets a server correctly distinguish a new write that *causally extends* one sibling from one concurrent with others, keeping the number of siblings bounded by the degree of true concurrency while using only O(#replicas) space. (Related: **dotted version vector sets / DVVSets** compactly represent a set of siblings.)

### 2.3 Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) — as used in CockroachDB

**HLC** (Kulkarni, Demirbas, Madappa, Avva, Leone, 2014) combines physical and logical time in one timestamp `(l, c)`:
- `l` = the max physical-clock value observed so far (locally or via messages);
- `c` = a logical counter to break ties/causality when `l` doesn't advance.

Rules: on a local/send event, if local physical time `pt > l` then `l := pt, c := 0`, else `c += 1`. On receive with `(l', c')`: `l := max(l, l', pt)`; `c` is set based on which argument supplied the max (`max(c, c')+1` if `l = l' = old l`, `c+1` if from self, `c'+1` if from message, `0` if `pt` won).

**Properties.**
- Satisfies the **logical-clock condition**: e → f ⇒ hlc(e) < hlc(f) (lexicographic on (l, c)).
- **Bounded drift from physical time**: `l ≥ pt` always, and `l − pt` is bounded by the clock-synchronization uncertainty ε (e.g., NTP offset bound); `c` is bounded too. So HLC timestamps are *meaningful as wall-clock times* within ε while remaining causally consistent.
- Fits in 64 bits (physical time in high bits, counter in low bits); monotonic even across NTP step adjustments; no blocking required.

**CockroachDB usage.** Every node carries an HLC; timestamps on transactions and MVCC versions are HLC values. Causality is propagated on every RPC (receiver ratchets its HLC), ensuring that causally related transactions get monotonically increasing timestamps. Because clock skew is only *bounded* (configured `--max-offset`, default 500 ms), not eliminated, CockroachDB handles reads in the **uncertainty interval** `[ts, ts + max_offset]`: if a read encounters a value with a higher timestamp inside its uncertainty window, the transaction performs an **uncertainty restart** (read refresh / timestamp push) to a higher timestamp, guaranteeing single-key linearizability and no **stale reads**. (CockroachDB provides serializable isolation; it does not guarantee strict serializability across non-overlapping transactions touching disjoint keys — the "causal reverse" caveat — precisely because it lacks TrueTime-style wait-out-the-uncertainty commit.) Nodes that detect clock offset beyond max-offset self-terminate to preserve correctness.

### 2.4 Contrast: TrueTime (Google Spanner)

**TrueTime** is *not* a logical clock — it's a tightly engineered **bounded-uncertainty physical clock** API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each datacenter. `TT.now()` returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain true absolute time, with ε typically 1–7 ms.

Spanner achieves **external consistency (strict serializability)** via **commit-wait**: a transaction with commit timestamp s waits until `TT.after(s)` is true (i.e., until s is definitely in the past, ~2ε) before releasing locks/acknowledging. This guarantees that if T1 commits (in real time) before T2 starts, then ts(T1) < ts(T2) — a property HLC-based systems cannot give without comparable hardware or explicit causality tokens. The trade-off triangle:

| | Lamport/Vector | HLC (CockroachDB) | TrueTime (Spanner) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hardware clocks needed | none | loosely synced (NTP), bounded skew assumed | GPS + atomic clocks |
| Captures causality | yes (vector: exactly) | yes (on message paths) | implicitly, via real time |
| Meaningful wall-clock time | no | yes, within ε | yes, within ε |
| Consistency achievable | causal / app-defined | serializable + single-key linearizable (uncertainty restarts) | external consistency via commit-wait |
| Cost of uncertainty | n/a | occasional transaction restarts | added commit latency (~2ε) on every write |

In short: Lamport clocks give a causality-*consistent* total order; vector clocks (and version vectors/DVVs for replicated data) give exact causality *detection*; HLC fuses logical causality with bounded physical time for MVCC timestamping without special hardware; TrueTime buys external consistency by shrinking and then *waiting out* physical uncertainty with specialized hardware.

# LSM Trees

**Core architecture.** A Log-Structured Merge tree buffers writes in an in-memory, sorted structure called the memtable, typically a skiplist (RocksDB, Cassandra) or a red-black tree. Every write is first appended to a write-ahead log (WAL) for durability, then inserted into the memtable. When the memtable reaches a size threshold, it is made immutable and flushed to disk as a Sorted String Table (SSTable): an immutable, sorted run of key-value pairs with an index block, filter block, and metadata footer. Reads consult the memtable, then immutable memtables awaiting flush, then SSTables from newest to oldest. Deletes and overwrites never modify SSTables in place; obsolete versions are reclaimed by compaction.

**Compaction strategies.**
- **Leveled compaction (LCS / RocksDB default).** SSTables are organized into levels L0 through Ln, where each level is roughly T times (commonly 10x) larger than the previous. Within L1+, SSTables have non-overlapping key ranges, so a point read touches at most one SSTable per level. Compaction picks an SSTable in Li, merges it with the overlapping SSTables in Li+1, and rewrites them. L0 is the exception: flushed memtables land there with overlapping ranges, so reads must check every L0 file. Leveled compaction minimizes space amplification (roughly 1.1x steady state) and read amplification, at the cost of high write amplification, approximately T per level, so O(T x levels) total.
- **Size-tiered compaction (STCS / Cassandra default).** SSTables of similar size are grouped into tiers; when a tier accumulates N (typically 4) similarly sized runs, they are merged into one larger SSTable in the next tier. Write amplification is low, O(log N) rewrites per entry, but key ranges overlap across runs, so reads may probe many SSTables, and space amplification can approach 2x or worse because duplicate versions of a key survive across tiers until merged.
- **Time-window compaction (TWCS, Cassandra).** Designed for time-series data with TTLs. SSTables are bucketed by write-time windows; STCS runs within the active window, and each expired window is compacted into a single SSTable that is never merged across windows. Whole SSTables can be dropped when all data in them expires, making deletion essentially free and avoiding tombstone-driven read degradation.

**Read-path accelerators.**
- **Bloom filters.** Each SSTable carries a Bloom filter over its keys (or key prefixes). A point lookup tests the filter before touching the SSTable; a negative answer (no false negatives) skips the file entirely. With ~10 bits per key, false-positive rates around 1% are typical, cutting read amplification for non-existent keys from one I/O per sorted run to nearly zero. Monkey (Dayan et al., SIGMOD 2017) showed optimal memory allocation gives more bits per key to lower levels. Bloom filters do not help range scans, which must consult every overlapping run; RocksDB offers prefix Bloom filters as a partial remedy.
- **Fence pointers.** An in-memory (or partitioned block-index) array holding the first key of each data block in an SSTable. A lookup binary-searches the fence pointers to identify the single block that could contain the key, bounding each SSTable probe to one block read instead of a scan or multi-block binary search on disk.

**Amplification tradeoffs and the RUM conjecture.** The RUM conjecture (Athanassoulis et al., EDBT 2016) states that an access method cannot simultaneously be optimal in Read overhead, Update (write) overhead, and Memory/space overhead; improving two degrades the third. LSM variants trace this tradeoff curve: leveled compaction buys low read and space amplification with high write amplification; size-tiered compaction buys low write amplification with high read and space amplification. Hybrid designs (Dostoevsky's lazy leveling, RocksDB's tiered+leveled mix) sit between. Write amplification matters doubly on SSDs because it consumes bandwidth and flash endurance.

**Tombstones.** A delete writes a tombstone marker that shadows older versions during reads and merges. A tombstone can only be purged when it is guaranteed no older version of the key exists in any lower level, which in leveled compaction means it has reached the bottom level, or in Cassandra after `gc_grace_seconds` (which also guards against resurrecting data on nodes that missed the delete, i.e., replica repair concerns). Accumulated tombstones inflate space and slow range scans, since scans must read and discard them; Cassandra exposes tombstone warning/failure thresholds for exactly this pathology. Range tombstones (RocksDB's DeleteRange) mark whole key intervals with a single marker.

# B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splits, merges, and rebalancing.** An insert into a full leaf splits it into two nodes and posts a separator key to the parent; splits can cascade to the root, which is the only way a B+tree gains height, keeping it perfectly balanced. Deletion that drops a node below the minimum fill (classically half-full) triggers either redistribution, borrowing entries from a sibling and updating the parent separator, or a merge with a sibling, deleting the separator from the parent, which may cascade upward and shrink the tree at the root. In practice, most engines (including InnoDB and PostgreSQL) implement lazy or deferred deletion: underflowing nodes are tolerated, and a page is reclaimed only when completely empty, because strict rebalancing on delete is rarely worth the latching cost (Johnson & Shasha's analysis supports free-at-empty).

**Latch coupling (crabbing).** The standard concurrency protocol for in-place B+trees. A traversal holds the latch on the parent, acquires the latch on the child, verifies the child is "safe" (won't split for inserts, won't merge for deletes), and only then releases the parent. For reads, the parent latch is released as soon as the child latch is acquired. Optimistic variants take shared latches down to the leaf assuming no structural modification, and restart with exclusive latches if the leaf proves unsafe. Modern in-memory variants replace latches with version validation (optimistic lock coupling, OLC).

**B-link trees (Lehman-Yao, 1981).** Each node carries a right-sibling pointer and a high key (upper bound of the node's key range). A split proceeds in two atomic half-steps: first create the new right node and link it via the sibling pointer, then post the separator to the parent. A concurrent reader that arrives at a node and finds its search key greater than the high key simply follows the right-link, so the tree is correct even between the two half-steps. This means traversals need to hold at most one latch at a time, no latch coupling on the descent, giving near-latch-free reads. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman-Yao B-link tree with the Lanin-Shasha deletion refinements.

**Sibling pointers.** Leaf nodes are chained into a doubly linked list (singly, right-only, in strict Lehman-Yao), enabling efficient range scans and ordered iteration without re-descending from the root, and enabling the B-link split protocol above. The cost is that splits and merges must update neighbors, and backward scans in a right-link-only design require care (PostgreSQL re-verifies left-links because they are not protected by the Lehman-Yao invariant).

**Prefix and suffix truncation (Bayer & Unterauer, "prefix B-trees", 1977).** Two compression techniques for separator keys and interior nodes. Suffix truncation: when a leaf splits, the separator posted to the parent need only be the shortest string that divides the two halves, not a full key, so "Johnson"/"Jonas" can be separated by "Jon". Shorter separators raise interior-node fanout, reducing tree height. Prefix truncation: keys within a page share a common prefix stored once per page, with entries storing only the distinct remainder. PostgreSQL added suffix truncation in v12 and page-level deduplication in v13; InnoDB uses page-level prefix compression in COMPRESSED/"index prefix" forms.

**Fill factor and page-split heuristics.** The split point chosen on page overflow determines long-run space utilization and depends on the insert pattern:
- **50/50 split (default random-insert behavior).** Splitting at the midpoint yields ~69% (ln 2) average page utilization under uniform random inserts.
- **Sequential-insert optimization.** Under monotonically increasing keys, a 50/50 split leaves every left page half-empty forever. Engines detect rightmost (or leftmost) splits and split asymmetrically: InnoDB tracks the insert direction per page and, on an ascending pattern, performs a ~90/10 or "split at insert point" so the old page stays nearly full and new rows go to a fresh page, yielding ~90%+ utilization for append workloads. PostgreSQL applies the same rightmost-page fast path ("fillfactor split" at the configured leaf fillfactor, default 90).
- **Configured fill factor.** Indexes can be built below 100% fill (InnoDB leaves 1/16 of a page free, `innodb_fill_factor` tunable; PostgreSQL index fillfactor default 90) to absorb future random inserts and HOT-style updates without immediate splits. Too low wastes space and cache; too high causes split storms under update-heavy load.

**Summary of contrasts.** LSM trees convert random writes into sequential I/O and defer reorganization to background compaction, paying in read and space amplification managed by Bloom filters, fence pointers, and compaction-strategy choice. B+trees update in place with logarithmic structural maintenance, paying in random write I/O and latch coordination, which B-link right-links, crabbing, truncation, and split heuristics mitigate. Both sit on the RUM tradeoff surface at different points: LSM favors updates, B+trees favor reads.
